Clinical Vignette: Layla

Layla sits with her hands folded in her lap, her calloused palms facing upward—the hands of someone who has spent three decades working with her body. At fifty-five, she carries herself with the quiet competence of a woman who has learned to rely on herself. She is an HVAC technician, one of the few women in her field in this region, and she takes pride in her work. But today, she struggles to meet my eyes as she begins to tell her story.

She was twenty-five when the war came to her neighborhood in Damascus. She doesn't speak about the specific violence she witnessed, though her jaw tightens when she approaches those memories. What she does describe is the smell—dust mixed with something acrid she couldn't name—and the sound of her mother's voice calling her name as buildings collapsed around them. Her father had already disappeared months earlier. Her younger brother was gone too. She and her mother fled with nothing but the clothes they wore, walking for days until they reached a refugee camp in Jordan.

The camp was meant to be temporary. It lasted eight years.

Layla learned to fix things there. A Swedish aid worker taught her basic mechanical skills, and she discovered she had a gift for understanding systems, for seeing how parts connected. It gave her purpose when everything else felt purposeless. When she was eventually resettled in North America at thirty-three, she pursued HVAC certification with single-minded determination. Work became her anchor.

But anchors can fail.

Three years ago, while installing a heating system in a basement, Layla became trapped. A ductwork section collapsed, pinning her leg. The darkness, the confined space, the dust filling her lungs—something in her fractured. She was extracted within minutes, suffered only minor injuries, but something fundamental shifted. She no longer feels safe in enclosed spaces, though her job requires her to crawl into attics and basements regularly.

Now she experiences what she describes as "the panic." It strikes without warning. Her heart races, her hands shake, and she becomes convinced that she cannot breathe, that the walls are closing in. She has pulled over while driving to job sites because suddenly the truck felt like a coffin. She has turned down lucrative contracts because they involved basement work. Her business partner has noticed her declining jobs, and the financial pressure adds another layer of anxiety she carries silently.

Sleep is fragmented. She wakes at three or four in the morning, her shirt soaked with sweat, her mind replaying scenarios that didn't happen—the basement collapse becoming the camp being bombed, becoming her mother's hand slipping from hers. She has tried to push through, to work longer hours, to exhaust herself into sleep, but her body refuses cooperation.

The divorce five years ago means she lives alone in a small house she owns outright. No one knows the depth of her struggle. Her ex-husband, a kind man, simply couldn't understand why she couldn't "just move on" from things that happened so long ago. She has no close family—her mother died in the camp—and she has maintained distance from the few relatives who made it to this country. She tells herself this is strength, this ability to stand alone, but lately the solitude feels like another kind of confinement.

Layla is here because her doctor insisted. She doesn't believe talking will fix what was broken so long ago and so recently reinforced. But she is trying. She is here, hands folded, finally allowing someone to witness the weight she has been carrying.
